phonemes.desc: The diphthong οι [oi] bearing the Greek circumflex — a long falling pitch on the first syllable of Μοῖραι; transliterated Moî-.
Rolled rho, then the diphthong αι [ai]: the name ends bright and quick, “rye.”

pronunciation.approximation: 'MOY-rye' — one long falling note on the first syllable, then a bright quick ending; the plural of μοῖρα, 'portion.'

kin.label: Greek common noun
kin.form: μοῖρα (moîra), “portion, lot, fate” — the word the three sisters personify; every “share” of life is a moîra.

kin.label: Greek verb
kin.form: μείρομαι (meíromai), “to receive as one’s portion” — the denominative verb behind the lexicon’s etymology “Apportioners.”

kin.label: PIE root family
kin.form: *(s)mer-, “to allot, care for, remember” — the deep root that also gives Latin memoria and English “memory”: fate as what is fixed and known.

pronunciation.note: Μοῖραι is the plural of μοῖρα, “allotted portion,” from μείρομαι, “to receive one’s share.” The circumflex on the first diphthong is the distinctive mark that plain ASCII “moirai” erases, so the restoration qualifies as Tier 1. Roman tradition knew them as the Parcae.

domains.title: Moirai
domains.subtitle: Fate
domains.lead: The Moirai are the three Apportioners — Klōthō the Spinner, Lachesis the Allotter, and Atropos the Unturning — who spin, measure, and cut the thread of every life, god and mortal alike. Older than Zeus in one of their two genealogies, they are the one power even the gods do not govern: fate, portion, the measured length of a life.

cards.name: Klōthō, the Spinner
cards.desc: She spins the thread of life on her spindle; nothing that lives is exempt from her thread (Plato, Republic 10.617c).

cards.name: Lachesis, the Allotter
cards.desc: She casts the lots and measures each thread — the length of days dealt to every being at birth.

cards.name: Atropos, the Unturning
cards.desc: “She who cannot be turned”: her shears cut the thread, and her name becomes death itself in Greek usage.

cards.name: Above Even the Gods
cards.desc: Zeus is their advisor at most, never their master: Homer has them spin the fates of heroes at birth (Iliad 20.127–128; 22.209–213).

symbols.name: The thread
symbols.meaning: The life-thread each mortal receives at birth — spun, measured, and finally cut; the spindle is their oldest attribute in art.

symbols.name: Spindle and distaff
symbols.meaning: Klōthō’s working tools; on vase paintings the Moirai appear as household spinners, like the women of any Greek town.

symbols.name: The shears
symbols.meaning: Atropos’ implement — the cut no prayer delays; Greek and Roman funerary art borrows the image for death itself.

symbols.name: The scales of Zeus
symbols.meaning: In Iliad 22.209–213 Zeus weighs the fates (kēres) of Achilles and Hector in golden scales — the Moirai’s portion made visible.

symbols.name: The number three
symbols.meaning: Three sisters for three moments — beginning, middle, end; the triad that gives fate its complete, closed shape.

mythology.lead: The Moirai’s mythology is scattered across the whole of Greek epic and philosophy — a genealogy told twice, two births they attend out of jealousy and pity, a loophole a god must pay for, and a final Platonic vision that hands fate back to the chooser. Their stories are always about the same question: who, in the end, is responsible for a life?

myths.title: Daughters of Night — or of Zeus
myths.text: Hesiod gives the Moirai two mothers. In the Theogony 217–222 they are born of Nyx, Night, among the dark powers that plague mortals — a lineage that makes them older than the Olympians and accountable to no one. Later in the same poem (901–906), the Zeus who has overthrown his own father marches order into the cosmos by wedding Themis, “Right,” who bears him the Moirai and the Horai, the Seasons. The double genealogy is a theology in miniature: fate is either the brute lot dealt by night, or the portion assigned within a just government of the world. Later tradition chose the second — but never quite forgot the first. The myth means the Greeks could not decide whether fate preceded justice or was its instrument, and so they kept both births.

myths.title: The Delayed Labor of Alkmene
myths.text: Homer’s most personal scene for the Moirai comes in Iliad 19.91–133. When Alkmene was due to bear Herakles, Zeus boasted on Olympus that a child of his blood would be born that day, “lord of all his neighbors.” Hera, in jealous cunning, swore to make the boast true — and delayed the birth: she sent Eileithyia, goddess of childbirth, to sit with folded hands and crossed legs, holding back the labor, while she hastened the birth of Eurystheus, a seven-months child of the weaker line. Only when a servant girl, Galinthias, tricked Eileithyia into rising did Alkmene deliver. The story means that even the birth of Greece’s greatest hero hung on a technicality of fate: Zeus’ word was kept, and still Herakles grew up the servant of the weaker man born first.

myths.title: Meleager and the Fire-Log
myths.text: Iliad 9.529–599 preserves the oldest telling. When Queen Althaea of Kalydon bore Meleager, the Moirai appeared standing by her bed and announced that the boy would live only until the log then burning on the hearth was consumed. Althaea snatched the brand from the fire and hid it away, and her son grew to manhood — handsome, brave, the slayer of the Kalydonian boar. Years later, in the quarrel over the hide, Meleager killed her brothers; in grief and rage Althaea brought the log out and burned it, and her son died as the fire died. Phoenix tells the tale in the embassy to Achilles as a warning against wrath. The myth means that the length of a life is a physical object — and the people we love are the ones who keep it.

myths.title: Apollo Serves Admetos
myths.text: Apollo once served a mortal year for his sins — Admetos, king of Pherai, a just man. To repay his kindness, the god made the Moirai drunk: he begged them to spare Admetos, and in their cups they promised that the king would live if someone else died in his place. Admetos’ aged parents refused; his wife Alkestis did not. Euripides opens his Alcestis (1–27) with Apollo explaining the bargain, and the play that follows is its terrible accounting: Admetos, spared, watches every kinsman refuse the substitute death one after another, until his young wife steps forward and goes to the grave in his stead. Apollodorus (Library 3.10.4) and Hyginus (Fabulae 50–51) retell the story and name the king of Pherai; later Christian readers noted that the barter of lives sits at the edge of their own oldest story. The myth means that even a loophole in fate is a debt someone must pay — and the loopholes the gods grant mortals are written in somebody else’s life.

myths.title: Plato’s Spindle of Necessity
myths.text: Plato’s Republic ends with the myth of Er (10.614b–621d). The souls of the dead arrive at the plain of Forgetfulness, where the three Moirai sit at the throne of Necessity, singing — Lachesis of the past, Klōthō of the present, Atropos of the future — while the spindle of the cosmos turns. Each soul draws a lot fixing the order of choosing, then chooses its next life; Lachesis sends with each the daimōn it has chosen as guardian. When the choosing is done, each soul drinks from the river of forgetfulness and is born. The vision states the boldest thing Greek philosophy said about fate: the Moirai supply the menu, but the chooser is responsible — “the responsibility is the chooser’s; god is blameless” (10.617e).

lore.syncretism: Rome translated the Moirai as the Fata or Parcae — Nona, Decuma, and Morta, one for each month of gestation, which tells us where the Romans thought fate is decided: at the cradle. Their names passed into every European language as “fate” itself (Italian fato, French destin). Medieval Iceland and Ireland kept sisters of the same office — the Norns of the Prose Edda, who likewise shape and cut beneath the world-tree — and Shakespeare’s “weird sisters” in Macbeth descend from Old English wyrd, “fate,” through Holinshed’s chronicle: three women prophesying at the edge of a battlefield. In modern Greek, μοίρα simply means “fate.” The Moirai never needed a myth of conquest; every culture found them again.
lore.culturalLegacy: The Moirai were worshipped, if modestly. Pausanias (2.11.3) describes their sanctuary at Sicyon, where they stood with Zeus Moiragetes, “Leader of the Fates,” and they received cult at Delphi and in Athens. Plato has Socrates acknowledge them in his last words — “we owe a cock to Asklepios” (Phaedo 118a). Their lasting monument is linguistic: “fate,” “moira,” the fatalism of tragedy and the novel. The image of three women spinning proved indestructible — it survives in Macbeth’s witches, in the cradle-fays of European folktale, and in the modern idiom of the “thread of life.” To spin, to measure, to cut: the oldest job description in the world, and the one nobody escapes.
lore.extendedMeditation:
The Moirai are Greek theology’s quietest, most radical idea: that the universe has a budget. Every life is allotted — spun out, measured, cut — and neither prayer nor virtue can extend the thread by a single cubit, though in the Odyssey Zeus protests (and concedes) that mortals blame the gods for what their own recklessness brings. Homer already contains the argument the philosophers will spend four centuries having: is fate compulsion, or only foreknowledge?

Plato’s answer — that we choose our lives and the Moirai only hold the spindle — turns fate into freedom with a terrible caveat: the choice is made half-blind, drunk on forgetfulness. The Moirai thus stand exactly where Greek thought passes from myth to ethics. They ask the question every mortal asks at three in the morning — how long, why me, who decided — and they answer with their implements: it is spun, it is measured, it is cut; and between the measuring and the cutting, everything you are is up to you.

lore.archaeology: The Moirai are creatures of text and vase more than of cult: no great temple is theirs, though Pausanias records their sanctuary at Sicyon beside Zeus Moiragetes (2.11.3) and they shared altars at Delphi. In art they appear from the late sixth century BCE as three working women — spinners with distaff and wool basket, deliberately ordinary, the fates dressed like the neighbors. Attic and South Italian vase painters show them at the births of gods and heroes; on Apulian funerary vases of the fourth century they attend Hades and Persephonē, shears in hand, turning a household craft into the machinery of death. Epigraphy extends their metaphor into administration: the Greek city distributed land and office by lot (klēros, the same language of “portion”), so that the polis lived institutionally inside the Moirai’s image of the allotted share.
